title: Promoting C2+ Production from Electrochemical CO2 Reduction on Shape-Controlled Cuprous Oxide Nanocrystals with High-Index Facets
abstract: Morphology and crystal facet controlled Cu2O nanocrystals (NCs) including cubic Cu2O (c-Cu2O) NCs with {100} facets, rhombic dodecahedral Cu2O (d-Cu2O) NCs with {110} facets, and concave octahedral Cu2O (o-Cu2O) NCs with high-index facets, are prepared and employed as catalysts for the electrochemical reduction of CO2 to C2+ products (ethylene, ethanol, and n-propanol). In-situ Raman characterizations demonstrate that the surfaces of all three Cu2O NCs are rapidly converted to metallic Cu during CO2 reduction and re-oxidized to smaller-sized Cu2O NCs after tests. Specifically, the o-Cu2O catalyst reveals the highest Faraday efficiency (48.3%) and partial current density (17.7 mA/cm2) for C2+ products at -1.1 V vs. reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE) compared to c-Cu2O and d-Cu2O, which is competitive among the reported Cu and Cu2O catalysts. In addition, abundant crystal defects/grain boundaries and high-index facets are observed on the surface of reconstructed o-Cu2O, which may serve as the active sites and benefit the C-C coupling during CO2 reduction. This work provides a new strategy to achieve efficient C2+ production from electrochemical CO2 reduction via crystal facet regulation of

sections.heading: ABSTRACT
sections.text:
Morphology and crystal facet controlled Cu2O nanocrystals (NCs) including cubic Cu2O (c-Cu2O) NCs with {100} facets, rhombic dodecahedral Cu2O (d-Cu2O) NCs with {110} facets, and concave octahedral Cu2O (o-Cu2O) NCs with high-index facets, are prepared and employed as catalysts for the electrochemical reduction of
CO2 to C2+ products (ethylene, ethanol, and n-propanol). In-situ Raman characterizations demonstrate that the surfaces of all three Cu2O NCs are rapidly converted to metallic Cu during CO2 reduction and re-oxidized to smaller-sized Cu2O NCs after tests. Specifically, the o-Cu2O catalyst reveals the highest Faraday efficiency (48.3%) and partial current density (17.7 mA/cm2) for C2+ products at -1.1 V vs. reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE) compared to c-Cu2O and d-Cu2O, which is competitive among the reported Cu and Cu2O catalysts. In addition, abundant crystal defects/grain boundaries and high-index facets are observed on the surface of
reconstructed o-Cu2O, which may serve as the active sites and benefit the C-C coupling during CO2 reduction. This work provides a new strategy to achieve efficient C2+ production from electrochemical CO2 reduction via crystal facet regulation of Cu2O catalysts.
KEYWORDS: Cu2O nanocrystals; crystal facet engineering; high-index facets;
electrochemical CO2 reduction; electrocatalysis.

sections.heading: INTRODUCTION
sections.text:
The serious environmental concerns caused by over-exploitation of fossil fuels and
the consequently ever-increasing concentration of atmospheric CO2 have triggered considerable attention.1-2 Electrochemical reduction of CO2 into high-valued chemical feedstocks using renewable electrical energy sources is regarded as a promising
solution to solve these intractable challenges.3-6 Although CO2 reduction reaction (CO2RR) can generate diverse products such as CO, HCOOH, CH4, C2H4, C2H5OH, and C3H7OH, it is still exceptionally challenging to reach the high efficiency and selectivity toward value-added C2+ products with a high energy density.7-8 This is because coupling to C2+ products poses additional constraints on the reactions, such as the existence of multiple and adjacent reaction intermediates and complicated
proton-coupled electron transfers, which usually require a high overpotential and
sophisticatedly designed catalyst morphology/structure.9-10
Among various studied catalysts, Cu-based electrocatalysts could convert CO2 into hydrocarbons with acceptable efficiency and selectivity.11-14 Efforts to improve the
Faraday efficiency (FE) of C2+ products on Cu-based catalysts have focused on the optimizations of sizes, morphologies, compositions, and exposed crystal facets of
electrocatalysts.15-22 Recently, oxide-derived Cu catalysts have demonstrated superior
activity for the C2+ generation to metallic Cu, likely due to the in-situ formed active grain boundaries/defects and/or the residual Cu+ ions in the surface layers during the
electrochemical reduction process.18, 20, 23-27 The reconstructed Cu surface caused by
the electrochemical reduction of the original Cu2O during the CO2RR process is also suggested to benefit the C-C coupling toward C2+ products and suppress the competitive hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) during CO2RR.25 Previous studies on

Cu2O-based electrocatalysts for CO2RR mainly focus on the film thickness and crystallite size controls of Cu2O nanocatalysts.27-28 Compared to the size control, crystal facet regulation, especially the design of high-index facets with significant
amounts of atomic steps, edges, and unsaturated coordinated sites provides more
opportunities in developing catalysts with high activity and selectivity.29-32
Truncated-octahedral Cu2O nanoparticles enclosed by both {111} and {100} facets has exhibited enhanced selectivity for C2H4 production and the synergistic effect of different low-index facets is observed.21 However, there are few studies on the
correlations between the high-index facets of Cu-based catalysts and their CO2RR performance.9, 22
In this work, Cu2O nanocrystals (NCs) enclosed by different crystal facets, including cubic Cu2O (denoted as c-Cu2O) with {100} facets, rhombic dodecahedral Cu2O (denoted as d-Cu2O) with {110} facets, and concave octahedral Cu2O (denoted as o-Cu2O) with {511} high-index facets, are prepared and their facet-dependent CO2RR performance are systematically investigated. Interestingly, it is revealed that the surfaces of all three Cu2O NCs are rapidly reduced to metallic Cu during CO2RR and fragmented into smaller-sized Cu2O nanoparticles after CO2RR, as evidenced by in-situ Raman spectroscopy and transmission electron microscopy (TEM). Among
them, o-Cu2O catalyst exhibits an outstanding partial current density of 17.7 mA/cm2 and a maximum Faraday efficiency (FE) of 48.3% for C2+ products (i.e., ethylene, ethanol, and n-propanol) at -1.1 V vs. reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE), which is
significantly higher than that of c-Cu2O (32.8%) and d-Cu2O (31.6%). Structural analysis after long-term CO2RR measurements indicates the remaining high-index facets and the newly-formed crystal defects/grain boundaries on the o-Cu2O catalyst may account for its outstanding activity towards C2+ production.

sections.heading: RESULTS AND DISCUSSION
sections.text:
Structural Characterizations of NCs. Shape-controlled Cu2O NCs were synthesized by a modified water-bath method32 in an oil/water emulsion system with
different solution pH values (Figure 1a). During the synthesis, Cu2+ in the water
phase was gradually extracted into oleic acid to generate Cu(C17H33COO)2, and then the addition of NaOH caused the formation of the oil/water emulsion with blue
colour. When sodium ascorbate was added, Cu2+ was reduced to Cu2O in the micro-encapsulation of oleic acid molecules, and then grew into Cu2O NCs via an Oswald ripening process. With raising the solution pH by adjusting the amount of
NaOH solution, Cu2O NCs with different morphologies were obtained under a joint kinetic control by pH and oleic acid on the growth rate of different crystal facets.32-33
Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) images of three Cu2O NCs are shown in Figure 1b-d. The average edge lengths of o-Cu2O, d-Cu2O, and c-Cu2O NCs are ca. 287 nm, 231 nm, and 310 nm, respectively (Figure S1a-c). All the obtained Cu2O NCs are loaded on carbon for further use in electrochemical measurements.

Figure 2a presents the X-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns of different Cu2O NCs, which reveal five diffraction peaks at 29.6°, 36.5°, 42.4°, 61.5°, and 73.7°,
corresponding to (110), (111), (200), (220), and (311) planes of cubic Cu2O (JCPDF no. 65-3288), respectively. The diffraction peaks of all NCs are sharp and intense,
indicating their highly crystalline nature. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) is
used to characterize the Cu oxidation state of the catalysts (Figure 2b). The peaks in
the high-solution Cu 2p XPS spectra of the obtained Cu2O NCs located at 932.3 eV and 952.2 eV are corresponding to Cu(I) species.34 The surfaces of d-Cu2O and c-Cu2O NCs should be dominantly enclosed by {110} and {100} facets, respectively.32-33 While the SEM and Transmission electron microscopic (TEM) images of the o-Cu2O catalysts along [ 1 ] and [001] directions could fit well with a - 1 - 1 model of truncated concave octahedra with an included angle of 109° (Figure 2c-h),
indicating that the as-prepared o-Cu2O NCs mainly expose {511} high-index facets, along with {100}, {110}, {111} and {021} facets.27, 35 The atomic model of the {511}
facet indicates that the (511) plane can be viewed as a composition of (100) terraces
and (011) steps, as demonstrated in the previous studies.32, 36 The edges of o-Cu2O NCs reveal clear and well-defined lattice fringes according to the high-resolution
transmission electron microscopic (HRTEM) images (Figure S2), indicating the high
crystallinity of the particles.

Electrochemical Characterizations. Linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) curves of
o-Cu2O, d-Cu2O, and c-Cu2O catalysts in Ar- and CO2-saturated 1.0 M KCl solutions are displayed in Figure 3a. Obviously, all of the studied Cu2O catalysts exhibit prominent increased current densities in CO2-saturated electrolyte than those in Ar-saturated one, indicating their high intrinsic activity for electroreduction of CO2. Furthermore, o-Cu2O shows the highest current density in the CO2-saturated electrolyte among the three catalysts.
The potential-dependent FEs of diverse products for electroreduction of CO2 on the developed Cu2O catalysts are calculated and displayed in Figure 3b-d. The major products for CO2RR on three Cu2O catalysts at -0.8 V vs. RHE are H2 (FE > 30%), CO (FE > 15%), and HCOOH (FE > 45%). When the potential shifts negatively, the
formation of C2+ products (ethylene, ethanol, and n-propanol) is significantly promoted and the FEs of C2+ products reach maximum at -1.1 V vs. RHE. The total FEs of CO2RR on the three Cu2O catalysts are similar at -1.1 V with the highest values of ca. 75%, while d-Cu2O and c-Cu2O catalysts produce more C1 products (CO

and HCOOH) than that of o-Cu2O catalyst. Specifically, the FEs of C2+ products on o-Cu2O, d-Cu2O, and c-Cu2O catalysts at -1.1 V are 48.3%, 31.6% and 32.8%, respectively. These results illustrate that the o-Cu2O catalyst could benefit C-C coupling and display enhanced activity for C2+ products compared to d-Cu2O and c-Cu2O. Further decreasing the potential to -1.2 V would drastically enhance the evolution of H2 on all three Cu2O catalysts (FE > 40%). The enhanced total current densities of o-Cu2O NCs compared to other Cu2O catalysts (Figure S3a) also prove the improved CO2RR activity of o-Cu2O NCs. Constant potential electrolysis curves of o-Cu2O, d-Cu2O, and c-Cu2O electrodes at various potentials are presented in Figure S3b-d, indicating the respectable stability of all Cu2O NCs at the tested potential ranges during 1 h electrolysis. In addition, o-Cu2O catalyst possesses a much larger C2+ partial current density than that of d-Cu2O and c-Cu2O (Figure 3e), further certifying the improved C2+ selectivity of o-Cu2O for CO2RR. Specifically, the current densities towards C2+ products achieved on the o-Cu2O catalyst at -1.0 V and -1.1 V are 7.0 and 17.7 mA/cm2, respectively, which are nearly twice of the d-Cu2O and c-Cu2O catalysts. The CO2RR performance of the developed o-Cu2O catalyst towards C2+ products is competitive among the previously reported Cu and Cu2O catalysts (Table S1).

The electrochemically active surface area (ECSA) of the developed Cu2O catalysts were estimated based on the double layer capacitances of the electrodes. As shown in
Figure S4, the carbon paper supported o-Cu2O catalyst exhibits a larger double layer capacitance (76.6 mF/cm2) compared to d-Cu2O (62.1 mF/cm2) and c-Cu2O (58.9 mF/cm2). The o-Cu2O catalyst with a relatively larger ECSA could provide more

and FE for C2+ products after 12 h stability test slightly decrease to 34.4 mA/cm2 and 44.6%, which maintains 89.1% and 90.4% of the initial values, respectively.
However, for d-Cu2O (Figure S3e), the total current density and FE for C2+ products after 12 h stability test could only maintain 79.6% and 75.3% of the initial values, and
c-Cu2O retains 75.9% and 78.0% of the initial ones (Figure S3f), respectively.
Mechanism Discussion. Surface reconstruction usually occurs on oxide-derived
catalysts during CO2RR and the structural changes of the developed Cu2O NCs are investigated by SEM after stability tests. SEM images (Figure S5a-c) indicate that the
surfaces of all the Cu2O catalysts are obviously roughened due to the Cu2O electroreduction and fragmentation of the surface. Of them, o-Cu2O NCs reveal more obvious surface roughening and reconstruction compared to d-Cu2O and c-Cu2O. Figure S5d, S5e, and S5f present the SEM images of o-Cu2O after the 4th LSV scan, 1 h, and 12 h chronoamperometry tests at -1.1 V, respectively. No apparent difference
in the catalyst morphology can be observed, indicating that the reconstruction and
fragmentation of o-Cu2O occur quickly once the voltage is applied. Such observations can be corroborated by LSV measurements. Significant reduction peaks are observed
on the first LSV scans of all Cu2O catalysts in CO2-saturated 1.0 M KCl (Figure S6a). O-Cu2O catalyst reveals two peaks at -0.36 V and -0.60 V, while both d-Cu2O and c-Cu2O catalysts have only a single peak at ~-0.60 V. The extra peak of o-Cu2O NCs at -0.36 V may be attributed to the surface reduction of the high-index facets
exposed on o-Cu2O surface.37 Obviously, the LSV curves of all three Cu2O catalysts during the 2nd and 3rd scans are basically overlapped with no obvious reduction

Figure 4. In-situ Raman spectra of Cu2O during CO2RR at constant potential of -0.6 V vs. RHE in CO2-saturated 1.0 M KCl. 2D Raman mapping of (a) o-Cu2O, (b) d-Cu2O, (c) c-Cu2O. We also employed in-situ Raman spectroscopy to probe the evolution of the Cu2O catalysts during CO2RR at a constant potential of -0.6 V (Figure 4). Vibrational fingerprints corresponding to Cu2O at 221.6 and 635.9 cm-1 are detected in all three Cu2O catalysts at the start of the CO2 reduction (at 0 s).27 Importantly, these peaks begin to decay rapidly after 60 s and almost disappear after 220 s, indicating the rapid
reduction of the surface Cu2O to metallic Cu once the cathodic potential is applied. Among them, o-Cu2O exhibits the medium reduced rate with a moderate Cu2O peak at 221.6 cm-1 after 220 s. Due to the fact that different crystal facets reveal varied
reduction rates, this may be related to the existence and complex interaction of {100},

{110}, {111}, {021}, and {511} facets of o-Cu2O.27, 34 On the other hand, the higher reduced rate of d-Cu2O than c-Cu2O may stem from the lower coordination numbers of {110} facets than {100}. When performing CO2 reduction for all three Cu2O catalysts at a more negative potential of -1.0 V vs. RHE (Figure S7), similar tendency
can be obtained in Raman spectra with the rapid decaying of surface Cu2O peaks, further indicating the quick surface reconstruction during CO2RR.
Figure S8a presents the XRD patterns of different Cu2O catalysts after 12 h stability tests at -1.1 V vs. RHE. All Cu2O catalysts can still be indexed to cubic Cu2O (JCPDF no. 65-3288), indicating that the high crystalline nature and phase purity of
the Cu2O catalysts can be well maintained after the stability test. Thus, it is deduced that the electrochemical reduction and reconstruction of Cu2O catalysts during CO2RR mainly occur on their surfaces. XPS is used to characterize the Cu bonding configuration of Cu2O catalysts after stability tests (Figure S8b). The peaks in Cu 2p XPS spectra of Cu2O catalysts located at 932.5 eV and 952.4 eV may correspond to Cu(I) species.34 Since the binding energies of Cu2O and metallic Cu are close,21, 32 it is difficult to distinguish Cu(I) and Cu(0) and the surface Cu may also be easily oxidized
to Cu2O when being exposed to the air.
TEM images of the Cu2O catalysts after stability tests are presented in Figure 5a-c. The concave structure of o-Cu2O catalysts are still partly remained after stability tests with an included angle of 109°, indicating that {511} facets can be partially
maintained after CO2RR. Notably, the surfaces of Cu2O NCs are composed of aggregated nanoparticles with sizes of tens of nanometers (the nanoparticles
surrounding Cu2O with a lower Z contrast are KJ carbons). It is deduced that those newly formed Cu2O nanoparticles observed on the surface of Cu2O are derived from the quick re-oxidization of metallic Cu produced during CO2RR upon exposure to the

further proves the polycrystalline structure of o-Cu2O after CO2RR, along with the existence of (100), (110), (111), (200), (211), (220), (221) facets and newly formed
(311), (321), and (420) high-index facets. The lattice-resolved HRTEM and fast
Fourier transform (FFT) images (Figure 5d-f and Figure S9, 10) further suggest that
o-Cu2O possesses more complex crystal facets compared to d-Cu2O and c-Cu2O. In addition, several distorted lattice fringes and grain boundaries, which are probably
resulted from fragmentation process during CO2RR, are observed in o-Cu2O (Figure 5f and Figure S11). Such fragmentation process may provide more active sites for
C2+ production via creating intricate network of grain boundaries and crystal defects with more high-index facet exposure,17-18, 38-40 thus resulting in the enhanced CO2RR performance.

sections.heading: CONCLUSIONS
sections.text:
In summary, morphology controlled Cu2O NCs enclosed with high-index facets are prepared and employed as high-performance electrocatalysts for CO2RR to C2+ products. Extensive characterizations demonstrate the in-situ surface reduction of the
developed three Cu2O NCs and the consequent surface fragmentation process that leading to the formation of small Cu2O nanoparticles. During CO2RR, the o-Cu2O catalyst exhibits much enhanced efficiency and increased current density for C2+ production compared to those of d-Cu2O and c-Cu2O, and is stable over 12 h electrolysis at -1.1 V vs. RHE. The well maintained high-index facets in parallel with
the abundant active sites derived from the in-situ generated crystal defects/grain
boundaries of the o-Cu2O catalyst are suggested to account for the improved C-C coupling during CO2RR. This work may provide new insights into realizing efficient C2+ formation from electrochemical CO2 reduction via rationally crystal engineering of electrocatalysts.
